problem: Existing EQA systems use VLM-prompted frontier exploration that is blind to indoor structure (doors, hallways) and question-relevant rooms, and their memories (scene graphs or raw snapshots) are either computationally heavy or grow unboundedly; inference is also slow and rarely reported.
motivation: Real-world deployment of EQA agents needs fast per-step inference, compact memory and robust handling of multi-target questions. Humans use priors about which rooms are relevant and move through doors and hallways, which suggests exploration should be room-aware and structure-aware.
key_idea: Use an LLM to extract relevant rooms and visual targets, explore globally via door/narrow-opening frontiers and locally within relevant rooms, keep a fixed top-k visual memory per target scored by CLIP+VLM relevancy, and answer with CoT GPT-4o.
insight: The ablation on a 100-question HM-EQA subset shows doorway-guided frontiers matter most: replacing them with standard FBE drops SR from 76.0 to 67.0, while removing CLIP scoring (69.0), VLM scoring (72.0) or CoT (72.0) each also hurts. Structural priors plus cheap local models (7B Prismatic VLM, CLIP) give faster steps (2.54 s vs 2.94 s for Fine-EQA) with better accuracy.
method: Query parsing: an LLM extracts relevant room types R and visual targets T (implicit queries yield guessed rooms) to filter the search space; the agent first spins 360° to build an initial occupancy map.

Global Relevance Exploration: a TSDF-fused fixed-height voxel occupancy map is sliced at agent height, candidate narrow-opening voxels (doorways/hallways) are found by neighbor occupancy checks, clustered with DBSCAN, and centroids are kept in a priority queue (larger clusters, closer to unexplored areas first).

Room detection and entry: a local Prismatic-VLM 7B names the visible room at every step; if a relevant room is visible but the agent is outside, AM-RADIO+SigLIP language-aligned features give a heatmap contour whose centroid is projected via depth into a direction to enter.
Local Relevance Exploration: inside a relevant room the agent spins 360° to collect views and queries GPT-4o stop condition at each step while still facing a relevant region.

Bounded target-specific memory: per target T_m keeps the top-k observations by rel_vis = λ·CLIP cosine(target text, image) + (1-λ)·Prismatic-VLM P('yes') relevancy, so memory is M×k and constant over time (k=3 in the figure).
CoT question answering: GPT-4o receives the question and the M×k stored images and is asked to think step by step, giving a letter (multiple choice) or free-form answer.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, stop condition and final answering) + Prismatic-VLM 7B (frozen, room detection and relevancy) + CLIP + AM-RADIO/SigLIP; LLM for query parsing
setting.action_space: discrete pose changes (translation up to 3 m per step, rotation) toward selected frontier/room-direction waypoints
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D scenes) for HM-EQA, MT-HM3D, EXPRESS-Bench, OpenEQA A-EQA

numbers.extra: mean ± std over 3 trials, temperature 0; max 3 m per translational step

numbers.evidence: Table 1, EXPRESS-Bench columns: 68.7 ±0.5 LLM Score, 29.25 ±0.55 E_path

numbers.extra: ablation subset, not the full set

numbers_note: Benchmark splits are not named in the paper (assumed val); OpenEQA metrics are LLM-Match not SR. Table baselines omitted.
results: FAST-EQA reaches 69.2 SR on HM-EQA (vs 63.5 Graph-EQA) and 68.7 LLM Score on EXPRESS-Bench (vs 63.95 Fine-EQA), while being competitive on A-EQA (49.0 vs 52.6 3D-Mem) and MT-HM3D (50.5 vs 55.1 Memory-EQA). Average step time is 2.54 s vs 2.94 s for Fine-EQA (13.6% faster) and much faster than 3D-Mem (14.53 s) and Memory-EQA (15.89 s).
limitations: Bounded by the spatial reasoning of current VLMs and by GPT-4o answer variance, which can cause premature termination.
Uses more steps than several baselines (e.g., 0.65 vs 0.20 for Graph-EQA on HM-EQA), trading path efficiency for accuracy; multi-target questions remain challenging (MT-HM3D below Memory-EQA).
